t.1.1: Beloved, the season of summer has arrived, with its fierce sun and longed-for moon, its pools of water constantly stirred by bathers plunging in, its evenings delightful, and Manmatha grown calm.
t.1.2: In the hot season, O beloved, nights whose dark streaks are dispelled by the moon, here and there a wondrous pavilion cooled by fountains, jewels of many kinds, and moist sandal paste become the things people seek to enjoy.
t.1.3: In the bright midnight, lovers enjoy a well-perfumed, charming palace rooftop, wine set trembling by the breath from their beloved's mouth, and song sweet with fine strings that kindles the fire of Madana.
t.1.5: By the feet of broad-hipped women, deeply tinged with the color of lac juice and adorned with anklets that at every step imitate the cry of the haṃsa, the hearts of men are filled with love.
t.1.4: With the round orbs of their hips wrapped in fine silk and girdles, with breasts bearing necklaces and ornaments and smeared with sandal paste, and with hair perfumed by fragrant bathing powders, women soothe the summer heat of their lovers.
t.1.6: Breasts smeared with sandal paste and crowned with necklaces as white as frost, and hips girdled with golden belts: whose mind do they not fill with longing?
t.1.7: Now, women in the flush of youth, their breasts high and the joints of their limbs beaded with rising sweat, cast off their heavy garments and lay only a thin silken cloth upon their breasts.
t.1.9: On summer nights, in the white mansions, the moon gazes long at the faces of women sweetly asleep, and, surely stirred by intense longing, at the night's end he turns pale, as if from shame.
t.1.8: By breezes stirred from fans moistened with sandal-scented water, by strands of necklaces laid upon the round breasts, and by songs sung in soft, sweet notes to the lute, Manmatha, as though asleep, is now being awakened.
t.1.10: The earth, its circles of dust whirled up by unbearable winds and scorched by the blazing heat of the fierce sun, cannot even be looked upon by travellers far from home whose hearts are burned by the fire of separation from their beloveds.
t.1.11: Deer, fiercely scorched by the blazing sunshine, their palates parched by a great thirst, catch sight of the sky, dark like crushed collyrium, and rush off toward another part of the forest, thinking, “There is water!”
t.1.12: With their flirtatious airs and smiling sidelong glances, playful women swiftly kindle the fire of Anaṅga in the hearts of travelers far from home, just as the evenings do, lovely with the moon as their ornament.
t.1.14: His zeal for valorous attack crushed by a mighty thirst, panting again and again with his mouth gaping wide, his tongue lolling and the tips of his mane quivering, the lord of beasts does not kill the elephants, though they are near.
t.1.13: Fiercely scorched by the sun's rays and burned on the path by the heated dust, the serpent, face bowed down, moving crookedly and breathing heavily again and again, settles down beneath the peacock.
t.1.15: Scorched by the rays of the sun, the elephants, spray rising from their parched throats, stricken by ever-growing thirst and longing for water, do not fear even the lions.
t.1.16: Wearied in body and mind by the sun's rays, which blaze like a fire fed with oblations, the birds do not strike the snake lying close beside them, its head tucked into the circles of the peacock's spread tail.
t.1.17: Fiercely scorched by the rays of the sun, a herd of boars digs with the broad discs of their long snouts into a pond grown with bhadramusta sedge, its mud all dried up, and seems to be burrowing into the very earth.
t.1.18: Scorched by the sun, wreathed in a garland of ever fiercer rays, a frog leaps up out of the pond with its muddy water and sits down beneath the parasol of a thirsty serpent's hood.
t.1.19: The lake has been made, by elephants crowded together and jostling one another, into a place whose whole tangle of lotus stalks is torn up, whose fish have perished, whose cranes have fled in fear, and whose mud is churned thick by their trampling.
t.1.21: Their mouths smeared with foamy slaver, their reddish tongues lolling out, faces upturned, tormented by thirst, a herd of buffalo cows has come forth from a mountain cave and gazes about for water.
t.1.20: The hooded serpent, the radiance of its crest-jewel kindled by the sun's rays, licking at the wind with its flickering forked tongue, scorched by the fire of its own venom and the blazing heat of the sun, and tormented by thirst, does not strike at the swarm of frogs.
t.1.22: Their young shoots of grain parched by the fierce heat of forest fires, their withered leaves tossed up by the force of harsh winds, their waters dwindled under the scorching sun, the forest tracts on every side inspire great fear in those who behold them.
t.1.23: The flock of birds pants, perched on trees with withered leaves; the weary troop of monkeys goes to the mountain's thicket; the herd of gavaya wild oxen wanders everywhere in search of water; and the unswerving herd of śarabhas draws up water from a well.
t.1.25: Swelled by the wind, the forest fire blazes in the caves of the mountains; it crackles with sharp reports in the tracts of dry bamboo; gaining strength in an instant, it spreads through the midst of the grass, and, clinging to the borders, it torments the herds of deer.
t.1.24: In every direction the lands are scorched by fire, which glows like freshly blossomed safflower and bright vermilion, rushes swiftly with a speed roused by the force of fierce winds, and flickers restlessly as it embraces the tips of the branches and creepers along the banks.
t.1.27: Elephants, gayals and lions, their bodies scorched by the fire, gather together like friends, casting aside their mutual enmity; worn out by the blaze, they swiftly leave the thicket and enter the river with its broad sandy banks.
t.1.26: Grown as if far mightier in the forests of śālmali trees, it flickers gold-bright in the hollows of the trees; leaping up onto the tall trees whose branches bear withered leaves, the fire, fanned by the wind, roams everywhere at the forest's edge.
t.1.28: May your summer, its waters strewn with lotus groves, delightful with the fragrance of pāṭala blossoms, with pleasant sprinklings of water and with moonbeams and necklaces to be enjoyed, pass happily for you in the company of loving women, at night on the terrace of a mansion where sweet songs are sung.
